resources.string: App developer · Engineering manager · All around cool dude
I build mobile apps and I lead the teams that make them.

I am an app developer, and currently an Engineering Manager at Insulet. I have been making mobile apps for %1$s years, and have been an engineer for %2$s. I like my cats, TV shows, single player story-driven games, and avoiding conversations about hobbies so people don't think I am boring. I dislike billionaires, inequality, and hateful people. I also dislike people who appear in the Epstein files.\n\nWhen I am not writing code at work, I spend a lot of my time figuring out how to make the workday as smooth as possible. I am a huge proponent of effective communication, and hate the overly formal and rigid structures that a lot of companies try to use in the workplace. Real speed and efficiency comes from letting your developers do what they do best and giving them the tools and appropriate structure needed to do that. There is no one-size-fits-all approach, and even each team in a company will be different.
Projects I've made on my own, over a decade of mobile work on apps that serve millions, and my education.
I can't have a personal website without showing off the things that matter most: my partner, Stella, and my cats, Storm, Lupin, Grey Thing, and Broomhilda.

Though this website is mostly a portfolio of things I have done, the state of the world compels me to also use it as a soapbox. Since I was a teenager I have had a very strong moral compass. I really value equality and kindness and empathy over anything. When I filled out my US Census form in college, I wrote in "human" as a race because I think that is where the world needs to be. We are all here sharing this planet together. Borders are imaginary, and the earth is such a small part of the universe as a whole.

But now more than ever we are being grouped and divided. It is like we haven't learned anything at all and wars are still being waged over stories told by desert farmers thousands of years ago. And if it isn't beliefs, it is ideologies, or skin color, or economic situations. Just anything to attack our neighbors; the ones we share a common history with. If you go back far enough in history, we all have a shared origin, so why are there so many arbitrary definitions of what makes us different from each other when, at the core, we are all the same?

The US is currently being run into the ground and divided by a group of hateful bigots led by a small, angry man. Respect is out the window, and he has been able to prey on the innate animal fear of something different from yourself, causing previously kind and caring people to turn into rude, racist, prejudiced, and entitled individuals. A cadre of pedophilic liars has created a cult to manipulate people into their own personal army of hate under the guise of politics. The utter dismantling of the trust of both the government and the foundations of science will not affect just America, because it is something that can spread like a disease if we let it.

Getting into specifics would make this much too long, and I would have trouble keeping this updated since there are new atrocities every day. We need to use our voices to fight this. We need to use our voices to fight for our neighbors. We need to use our voices to fight for science, and for reason, and for kindness. We need to use our voices to unite! The enemy is not the person who lives across the street. The enemy is the idea that the person who lives across the street is your enemy. The enemy is the people who are spreading that idea. Those people — the ones who control 99% of the resources — are the ones we need to stand up against. There are so many more of us than there are of them, and if we could all speak together we could not be beaten.

If you read this, thank you, and please speak up somewhere. If you read this and you disagree, please do some real introspection to figure out why you feel this way, and realize that somebody else has told you to be angry. You do not have to be hateful, that is your own choice. Which side of history do you want to be on?
Side projects, the jobs I have had, and the degree that I barely even use anymore.

PICKY is a collaboration between me and tattoo artist Gunnar V. The idea is to let tattoo artists focus on their art by making all of the other stuff a lot easier.

The app handles things like client and ink management, helps you pick which inks to use to tattoo an image, and helps you mix inks to make other colors. It also has a handful of built-in algorithms for making stencils specifically for tattooing, and you can print those stencils straight from the app.

PICKY started out as a Compose Multiplatform app made mostly for iPads, but I have since rewritten it as a pure SwiftUI app that supports iPads, iPhones, and macOS.

I also have a Linux server I tinker with. This helps me make sure I'm only mostly super specialized in app development. It has the added benefit of me being able to understand up to half of what the backend and dev ops people are talking about in meetings!\n\nI use Mint because I'm afraid of headless (go ahead, judge me) and manage all of my services with Docker. I manage a bunch of things for my household like a personal media server, home automation, and a private cloud. It is also a fun testing ground for me to try out other things like self-hosted LLMs.

Breez is an app for keeping a household in sync. It puts all of the everyday stuff you share with a partner in one place: a grocery list, a pantry, recipes, to-dos, and notes. The fun part is that it is all connected. When you check something off the grocery list it goes straight into the pantry, and since the recipes know what is already in the pantry, the app can suggest what to make for dinner with what you have.

Everything lives in a "space" that you share with someone by scanning a single-use QR code. The app is offline first, so it writes everything to a local database and syncs from there. That means it works fine without a connection and just catches up when it gets one. It is completely usable on a single device, and a subscription adds syncing and sharing. There are no ads, no tracking, and I am not selling your data.

Breez is built with Compose Multiplatform, so Android, iOS, and web all come from one codebase.

HelpMyCity is an open source issue tracker that any city can fork and run. A resident reports a problem (a pothole, a dead streetlight, a blocked sidewalk ramp, that kind of thing), a community manager triages it, and then everyone can follow along until it gets fixed. I wanted something better than the old-school white-label solutions that nobody actually enjoys using. It is built for cities that lean on volunteers, since per-seat pricing doesn't really scale when a lot of your help isn't on the payroll.

It is also about making city work more transparent. Usually a report disappears into some city request system that residents can't see into, and you just have to hope somebody gets to it. Here, everyone can watch it move along. If an issue gets rejected, it always comes with a reason the resident can read. Every status change and review decision is kept as history on the issue, and when something needs official action, the city's own reference number gets recorded right on it. Approved issues show up in a searchable list, on a kanban board, and on a map.

Just like Breez, the app is offline first and built with Compose Multiplatform. It stores everything in a local database and syncs with the backend, so it works just as well with no signal, and Android, iOS, and web all come from one codebase. All of the city-specific and backend-specific decisions live in one replaceable module, so if you want to fork it for your own town, that module is the only thing you have to touch. The demo at helpmycity.dev runs on Supabase and is set up for Oceanside, CA.
Saint Rose, Louisiana, USA and Kongsberg, Norway

Kongsberg Maritime makes technology for ships and offshore vessels, and it is probably best known for its dynamic positioning (DP) systems. DP is basically cruise control for staying in one spot: a computer uses the vessel's own propellers and thrusters to hold its position and heading against wind, waves, and currents. Their K-Pos systems are used on everything from drill ships to cruise liners, for jobs where dropping an anchor or tying up just isn't an option.

I first worked for Kongsberg Maritime as an intern in 2012, the summer before my senior year of college, mostly on dynamic positioning software. After graduating I came back full-time as a System Engineer, working on the software control systems of vessels all over the world. That meant traveling out to the vessels themselves to do maintenance or upgrades. Eventually I got specialized training in thruster control systems and moved to Norway to be a Project Engineer, configuring dynamic positioning and thruster control systems for brand new vessels. I would set up the systems from scratch, run lab tests with the client and DNV (the registrar and classification society), and then travel out to commission the vessel on a sea trial. This job taught me how to work in a really high-stress environment where the quality of your work matters a lot, since doing a bad job could have environmental consequences.

Holte makes mobile and web software for construction companies. The idea is to handle the paperwork side of a construction project right from the job site: project management, tracking time and materials, and quality assurance. Their apps, like HoltePortalen, let project managers and workers look up project info, log their hours, and document progress with photos and attachments, so everyone on the project is working from the same up-to-date information.

Holte was my first job as an app developer, which up until then was something I had only done as a hobby. The company used Xamarin Native at the time, so I was working with the native Android and iOS APIs through a C# wrapper. While I was there we had a suite of 5 different apps and a dashboard app that tied them all together. We had shared libraries for things like the network stack and storage, but the UI was all native. The company didn't have any mobile designers either, so I ended up taking that on myself.

NRK (the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation) is Norway's public broadcaster, kind of like the BBC of Norway. Besides its TV and radio channels, it runs NRK TV, a streaming service with a huge library of series, documentaries, news, and films. It doesn't cost anything to watch in Norway, which fits NRK's whole mission of making media accessible to the entire population.

At NRK I mainly worked on the NRK TV streaming app for Android TV and other Android devices. This was my first job using Kotlin in a fully native Android environment. Besides being on the Android team for NRK TV, I was also fagansvarlig (which loosely translates to technical lead) for the group of mobile app developers at NRK. The things I am most proud of from my time there are the custom Android TV framework we built because Leanback was too restrictive, and a Kotlin Flow-based login library that could be shared across the mobile apps. Since NRK is a public service, there was also a big focus on accessibility and universal design.

Vipps is the go-to payment app in Norway. It was started by a group of Norwegian banks, and it lets you send and receive money with just a phone number instead of bank account details. It has grown way past paying your friends back, though. You can use it to pay online and in stores, pay bills, and even log in to websites and services. It is so baked into everyday life in Norway that people use it for basically everything, from splitting a restaurant bill with friends to paying at the local store.

I was at Vipps as a consultant during COVID, when the whole world had to figure out how to work again. I was on the Vennebetaling team, which handled the peer-to-peer side of the Vipps app. While I was there, my vertical-slice team (product, backend, QA, Android, and iOS) rewrote the entire groups and settlements features from the ground up. That is the functionality behind sharing and splitting payments with friends. Besides that, one of my main focuses was pushing the app into the Jetpack Compose era, back when we were using alpha and beta libraries and nobody had really figured out the best practices yet. I also spent a lot of time on animations and trying to make the app feel more "fun".

BankID is the leading electronic ID and digital signature solution in Norway, and over 4 million people use it. You need it for pretty much everything: logging in to your bank or government websites, signing legally binding documents, and approving payments. The mobile app lets you prove who you are with your face or fingerprint instead of carrying around one of those little code generators. It even has a digital ID card now, so you can use it at the post office when picking up a package or at the liquor store to prove you are old enough.

Besides being an Android developer, I was the engineering manager for all of the app developers at Stø, which was 5 Android and 5 iOS developers. As a leader and a member of the App Foundation team, I spent a lot of my time coordinating with the different product teams to keep a big-picture view of the app, both from a user's perspective and a developer's perspective. I worked on pretty much every part of the app, building core pieces like the network stack and the design system, and rearchitected a lot of it around Jetpack Compose and modern best practices. I also suffered through the flaky Android keystore and other security-related parts of the app, the most important being our new DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) security architecture.
Insulet is a global company that makes the Omnipod, a tubeless insulin pump for people with diabetes. Instead of a pump hooked up with tubing, it is a small Pod that you wear.

I manage the DevX tools team, a team of mobile developers that build internal tools for the other developers in the company. We use Kotlin Multiplatform to make libraries that simulate Insulet's hardware, which makes development and testing a lot easier for everyone else.
Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering

When I was starting college, I was very close to going into chemical engineering, because I loved chemistry. But the advisor told me being color blind could cause problems, so I took my interest in electronics and computers and went into electrical engineering instead. I spent my college years taking classes like circuits, microprocessors, optical electronics, control systems, and microfluidic biochips. I also took two semesters of C++, which made me promise to never be a software developer. It wasn't until years later that I learned I didn't hate programming, I just hated C++.\n\nOutside of class I worked the electrical engineering department's help desk and spent some time as a network infrastructure technician for the university. I also was active in the LSU chapter of IEEE, eventually serving as President of the chapter during my senior year.
